one_liner: Header-only C99 SSE/AVX2 UTF-8 validator (2018) that validates at 0.45-0.7 cycles/byte versus about 11 for a branchy scalar loop.
what_it_does: Checks whether a byte buffer is valid UTF-8 using x86 SIMD. The API is a set of static C functions with the signature bool f(const char *src, size_t len): validate_utf8_fast (SSE), validate_utf8_fast_avx and validate_utf8_fast_avx_asciipath (AVX2), AVX-512 variants compiled only when AVX512F, VL and VBMI are enabled, plus ASCII-only checks validate_ascii_fast and validate_ascii_fast_avx. The result is a yes/no answer only: no error offset, no decoding and no transcoding.
how_it_is_fast: It works on 16 (SSE) or 32 (AVX2) bytes per step. A pshufb lookup on each byte's high nibble gives the expected sequence length, and two shifted saturating subtractions ('carry continuations') spread that length over the following bytes; comparing carried and initial lengths flags missing or extra continuation bytes, while separate vector compares catch bytes above 0xF4, overlong forms (C0/C1, E0 followed by less than A0, F0 followed by less than 90), surrogates (ED followed by more than 9F) and code points above U+10FFFF (F4 followed by more than 8F). Errors are OR-ed into one register across the whole buffer with no data-dependent branches, which removes the branch mispredictions that dominate scalar validators on mixed-length text. This is the 2018 predecessor of the Keiser-Lemire 'lookup' algorithm used in simdjson and simdutf; the paper the README cites describes that later algorithm, not this code.
when_to_use: Learning or teaching SIMD UTF-8 validation: the SSE validator is about 200 lines of commented C99 intrinsics in one header.
A C code base on known x86-64 hardware that can only take a single permissively licensed header (Apache-2.0, BSL-1.0 or MIT) and is built with fixed -msse4.1 or -mavx2 flags.
Bulk yes/no checks of buffers with many multibyte characters (tens of KiB), where a byte-at-a-time validator pays around 11 cycles/byte in branch misses.
A fast all-ASCII gate before a slower path: validate_ascii_fast_avx ran at 0.05 cycles/byte in the README run.
when_not_to_use: Production use: the README marks the library obsolete since 2022 and for demonstration only, and points to simdutf, which adds runtime CPU dispatch, ARM NEON, AVX-512 and the faster lookup algorithm.
Any non-x86 target (ARM, POWER, RISC-V): there is no implementation, and there is no runtime dispatch, so a binary built with -mavx2 or -march=native faults on CPUs without that ISA.
You need the error position, decoding or UTF-16/UTF-32 conversion: the functions return bool only.

Mostly-ASCII text with the plain SSE function: validate_utf8_fast ran at 0.704 cycles/byte on ASCII, slower than the repo's scalar eight-bytes-at-a-time ASCII check (0.104); use the AVX asciipath variant (0.088) or simdutf instead.
Short strings: only 64 KiB buffers were benchmarked, and the tail is copied into a zeroed 16- or 32-byte stack buffer on every call; small-input cost is not documented.

integration.min_toolchain: C99 (designated initializers), GCC or Clang with x86intrin.h; MSVC not documented. SSE path needs SSSE3 and SSE4.1 (pshufb, palignr, ptest); AVX2 variants need __AVX2__; AVX-512 variants need AVX512F+VL+VBMI. Makefile builds with -std=c99 -march=native -O3.
integration.platforms: x86-64 only (SSE4.1 minimum; AVX2 and AVX-512 VBMI variants selected at compile time); README says it does not work on ARM
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the validators are pure functions over the caller's buffer and keep no global state in the headers
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same bool validate(const char *, size_t) shape as the scalar validate_utf8 in the benchmark, but x86-only, chosen per ISA at compile time, and it never exits early on an error

gotchas: Harness flaw in the baseline: the scalar validate_utf8 in benchmarks/benchmark.c ('copied in part from Guava') ported Java's signed-byte test bytes[i] > (byte)0xBF as an unsigned > 0xBF, so ASCII bytes are accepted as continuation bytes: "\xC3\x28", "\xC2\x7F", "\xE2\x82\x28" and "\xF1AAA" all return true (a faithful Python model of the function misclassifies 3,840 of the 65,536 two-byte inputs, always by accepting invalid ones). tests/unit.c never runs it. On the all-valid benchmark input the timing is not affected, but the baseline is a lenient checker, not a reference validator.

The random-looking UTF-8 input is half ASCII spaces and half multibyte characters of random length, which maximises scalar branch mispredictions; the 15.6x and 24.5x gaps are a best case, and on mostly-ASCII text the SSE function's lead shrinks to 1.8x (and it loses to a word-at-a-time ASCII skip).

Current harness defects (after the README numbers): commit c0a5f7e (2024-03-13, issue #27) removed the out-of-bounds data[N] = '\0' write from populate(), but demo() still calls the Hoehrmann DFA validators with N + 1 on a malloc(N) buffer, so those rows now read one uninitialised byte past the allocation; the PR #26 fix for issue #25 scales tv_sec by 1E6 instead of 1E9, so the GB/s print is wrong whenever a run crosses a second boundary. Neither touches the README cycle counts, which predate both the DFA rows (2020) and the GB/s output (2020).
The 'double' DFA schemes the current benchmark also prints are known not to validate correctly (issue #24, warning printed by the program); ignore those rows.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Rarely: simdutf (catalogued under encoding) supersedes it on speed, platforms and testing, protobuf's utf8_range (range algorithm) adds NEON and beat a NEON port of this algorithm by about 1.32x in its own tables, and simdutf8 is the Rust choice; pick fastvalidate-utf-8 only for a tiny, readable, permissively licensed C99 x86 header or to study the original carry-continuations technique. In lemire/validateutf8-experiments the same algorithm ported to AVX2 ('basic' rows) ran at 13.1-15.5 GB/s on hongkong.html against 17.1-20.9 GB/s for the later lookup4, and at 6.4 versus 12.2 GB/s on random multibyte input (results/skylake.txt).
verified_claims_summary: On an unnamed Skylake with GCC (version not stated) and -std=c99 -march=native -O3, best of five rdtsc runs on 64 KiB buffers: random-looking valid UTF-8 took 0.702 cycles/byte (SSE) and 0.448 (AVX2) against 10.967 for the repo's byte-at-a-time Guava-derived scalar validator (about 15.6x and 24.5x), and pure ASCII took 0.704 and 0.450 against 1.256 (about 1.8x and 2.8x). The scalar baseline is not a standard-library function and, as noted, accepts some invalid input.
status_note: Stale, self-declared obsolete demonstration code (last commit 2024-03-13, a benchmark-only change); triple-licensed Apache-2.0, BSL-1.0 or MIT and small enough to vendor, but the author directs production users to simdutf.
